newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria struggling on against terrorism -president.
newsitem.headline: Algeria struggling on against terrorism -president.

text.p: Algerian President Liamine Zeroual said in Algiers on Tuesday that his government, which plans to hold local elections in October, would pursue its struggle against Islamist "terrorism" until it was finally wiped out.

In a 30-minute televised live speech in Arabic on the occasion of "Moudjahid Day" (national day) he said: "The Algerian state will pursue with determination and rigour its struggle against terrorism until final eradication."
Zeroual said political violence against civilians was a "wide conspiracy prepared against Algeria which failed in its objectives".

"The savage revenge against our people who resist terrorism recalls the revenge of (French) colonialists ...during the glorious revolution. The crimes committed against the Algerian nation confirm that terrorism in our country is experiencing its last hours as happened in the past."

Authorities in January 1992 cancelled the first round of legislative elections after Islamic fundamentalists took a huge lead. Violence erupted shortly afterwards and about 60,000 people have since been killed.
Since the last election on June 5, 1997, more than 700 people, including children and pregnant women, have been killed.
Zeroual said despite the political violence Algeria "will continue its elections process and hold local elections on October 23".
"Local elections, which will be marked by transparency and freedom, will be a new step towards institutional stability and strengthening of democratic practice," he said.
At the last local elections in 1990, candidates of the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) swept to power in more than half the country's town halls and 48 provinces.

The FIS went on to take a massive lead in Algeria's first multi-party general election in December 1991. The following month the authorities scrapped the poll and the North African nation plunged into violence.
The authorities outlawed the FIS and replaced its elected local and provincial councils with government appointees.
Earlier this month, Algeria held multi-party parliamentary elections from which radical Islamists were barred.
